MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

steps.title: Welcome to iLit
steps.text: iLit is a website for researching Canadian immigration case law. It gathers public court and tribunal decisions into one library, lets you search them, and shows each decision in a clean reader with the cases and statutes it relies on beside the text. It runs in an ordinary browser, with nothing to install. In this tour each step first tells you what I am about to do; press Next and I do it, then explain what you see. The bar at the bottom has Next, Back, Skip section and Exit.

steps.title: The library today
steps.text: These figures are read from the database as the page opens: the decisions in the library, the citations found in them, and the Federal Court immigration files held with their full docket history.

steps.title: Why it was built
steps.text: Immigration litigation is growing, and much of what would help is already public but scattered: decisions, docket entries and the authorities they cite sit on different websites, and the links between them are not shown. iLit brings that record together and connects it, so a question such as how the Court has treated an issue can be answered in minutes. It is a research aid; it does not give legal advice or predict results.

steps.title: Who it is for
steps.text: It is designed for the Canada Border Services Agency's work on immigration litigation, mainly the Hearings and Litigation Division. That is a design target, not an endorsement: the Agency has not adopted it. Anyone who reads immigration decisions for their work can use the same library.

steps.title: How it works
steps.text: Every decision takes the same path. It is collected from the public court and tribunal websites with its source link, split into numbered paragraphs, and read by fixed written rules that find the citations, statute references, judge, outcome and type of case. What the rules find is stored beside the original text. The same decision always gives the same answer, and no AI is called when you use the site.
steps.say: How it works explains where the decisions come from and how everything shown beside them is worked out. I'll open it.

steps.title: How each piece is worked out
steps.text: Citations, statutes, outcomes, case types and judges each have their own rules, described here with what they can and cannot do yet. Where the rules cannot tell, the site says so instead of guessing.

steps.title: The tour follows these tabs
steps.text: From here we go left to right: Research to find and read decisions, Intelligence / Statistics for judges, citations and Federal Court activity, then the Workbench and its document tools. At the end, how the library keeps itself current.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: Research is where work starts. One box takes a case name, a citation such as 2019 SCC 65, or words from the reasons. Filters narrow any search, and the results are listed below.
steps.lead: OK, let's move on to Research.
steps.leadText: I'll click Research in the header.

steps.title: A plain search
steps.text: Every decision whose reasons use those words is listed, with its court, date, judge, outcome and case type, and how often other decisions cite it. I won't open one yet; first, the filters.
steps.say: First, a plain search. I'll type best interests of the child and press Search.

steps.title: The filters
steps.text: The filters sit on the left, and all of them combine: outcome, court, case type, cases citing a given decision, topic tags, judge, Minister and year.
steps.say: Now the filters. I'll clear the search box and open Advanced.

steps.title: Outcome and court
steps.text: Outcome and Court are one click each. Government won and Individual won use the outcome recorded for each decision, and more than one court can be picked.

steps.title: Case type
steps.text: Each group opens to its types. Ticking the box beside a group selects every type in it at once; ticking a single line picks just that type. Case types are worked out from the provisions a decision applies, with no AI.
steps.say: Case type sorts every decision by the kind of case it is. I'll open the Refugee protection group.

steps.title: A topic tag
steps.text: Cessation is now a filter, shown under the box; the × removes it. Tags are the legal topics found in each decision, and the list shows how many decisions carry each one.
steps.say: Tags are the legal topics found in each decision. I'll type cessation in Tag and pick it.

steps.title: A second tag
steps.text: Tags combine: a decision must carry both, so the list will keep only cessation decisions involving India.
steps.say: Tags can be combined. I'll add India.

steps.title: Cases citing a decision
steps.text: Only decisions that cite Vavilov, the Supreme Court's leading case on the standard of review, will be kept.
steps.say: Cases citing keeps the decisions that cite a case you name. I'll type Vavilov and pick it.

steps.title: Run the search
steps.text: These are cessation decisions involving India that cite Vavilov and that the Minister won: four filters, one list. Words typed in the box would narrow it further.
steps.say: Last, who won. I'll press Government won, which runs the search with all four filters.

steps.title: The reader
steps.text: This is the decision in the reader: the text as a clean document with numbered paragraphs, and what iLit found in it around the text. The reader has three parts; I'll take them one at a time.
steps.lead: Let's open one of these decisions.
steps.leadText: I'll click the one this tour uses from here on.

steps.title: 1. The header
steps.text: The court, outcome and title; then the citation, case type, date, docket number and the judge. The counts on the right are the decisions that cite this one, the cases it cites and the statutes it refers to. Copy citation, the Federal Court file and Save to Workbench sit above.

steps.title: 2. The decision
steps.text: The decision itself, formatted, with numbered paragraphs. Citations are marked in gold, statutes and regulations in purple, and topic tags in green; the buttons above switch each colour on or off.

steps.title: 3. The side panel
steps.text: The side panel has three tabs. About holds the outcome, case details, the topics found in the text and the Outline. Authorities lists every case and statute the decision cites. Intelligence shows the judge and how this decision has been cited since.

steps.title: About
steps.text: The recorded outcome, with a link down to the part of the decision that disposes of the case, the case details, and the topics found in the text with how often each appears. Pressing a topic steps through the places it is mentioned.

steps.title: The Outline
steps.text: The Outline lists the decision's sections with the paragraph each starts at. It carries a Coming soon tape because section detection is not yet reliable on every decision.
steps.say: Further down is the Outline. I'll scroll to it and open it.

steps.title: Jump to a section
steps.text: The text moved to that section and marked it. The Outline is the quickest way to the analysis or the conclusion of a long decision.
steps.say: I'll press one of the sections.

steps.title: The judge, in a snapshot
steps.text: The Intelligence tab opens on the judge's profile: their decisions in the library, how often the government won before them, decisions per year and the most recent ones. Open full judge profile goes further.
steps.say: Now the judge. I'll click the decision maker's name in the header.

steps.title: How it has been cited
steps.text: Citation intelligence for this decision: how many decisions cite it and how often, the outcomes of those cases, citing cases per year and by court.
steps.say: Beside it is Citation intelligence. I'll open it.

steps.title: A citation, previewed
steps.text: The preview names the cited case and shows the paragraph this decision points to, taken from that decision in the library.
steps.say: Back to the text. Resting the pointer on a gold citation shows a preview. I'll move to one that names a paragraph.

steps.title: Open it as a card
steps.text: The card opens under the paragraph, with the cited passage in full. Its i button opens the cited case in the Intelligence tab, and double-clicking the citation opens that decision in a new tab.
steps.say: Clicking the citation keeps that passage open as a card. I'll click it.

steps.title: Pin it
steps.text: A pinned card stays put while you scroll and read on, so the passage can be checked against this decision's reasons. Clear pinned cards, above the text, removes them all.
steps.say: The pin keeps the card open. I'll pin it.

steps.title: A statute, previewed
steps.text: The preview shows the text of the provision, from the statute library.
steps.say: Statutes, in purple, work the same way. I'll rest the pointer on one.

steps.title: And as a card
steps.text: The card holds the provision. It pins the same way; its i leads to statute intelligence, which is marked Coming soon, and double-clicking opens the section in the statute library.
steps.say: I'll click it.

steps.title: Authorities
steps.text: Every case and statute the decision cites, with how many times and at which paragraphs. The arrow on a row shows the cited passage, and the filter at the top finds one quickly.
steps.say: Now the Authorities tab. I'll open it.

steps.title: Go to where it is cited
steps.text: Each press moved the text to the next place that case is cited and marked it. The counter shows which one you are on, and the up arrow goes back.
steps.say: Each row can take you to every place that authority is cited. I'll press the first row's button a few times.

steps.title: Search this decision
steps.text: Every match is marked in the text. The arrows, or Enter, step through them, with the count beside the box.
steps.say: Search this decision finds any word in the text. I'll type passport and step through the matches.

steps.title: Keep it on your Workbench
steps.text: The decision is now pinned to your own list on the Workbench, where we will find it later in the tour.
steps.writes: This step pinned Vavilov to the demo Workbench list called Demo analyst. Remove it any time from the Workbench.
steps.say: Last in the reader: Save to Workbench. I'll save this decision for you.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.text: The first Intelligence page. Every judge in the library is listed on the left with their number of decisions, the different spellings of a name merged into one.
steps.leadText: I'll click it in the header.

steps.title: One judge's record
steps.text: A profile shows the judge's decisions year by year, how the cases came out, and their most cited decisions.
steps.say: I'll open the judge with the most decisions.

steps.title: Citation Intelligence
steps.text: Citation Intelligence starts from one decision, here the cessation decision we read, and shows who relies on it: which courts and judges cite it, the outcomes of the cases that cite it, and how its use has changed year to year.

steps.title: Federal Court Analytics
steps.text: This page is built from the Federal Court's own registry for immigration files: every application for leave and judicial review as it was filed, including the many that end without published reasons, such as leave refused, discontinued or settled. Published case law only shows the files that reach written reasons. We know of nowhere else this is gathered and searchable.

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.text: The key numbers for whatever the filters select: files, how often leave and judicial review are granted, settlements, how long a leave decision takes, and stays of removal.

steps.title: What happens to a file
steps.text: Of the files filed, how many reach a leave decision, a hearing and a judgment, and how each year's files ended. This is the part no set of published decisions can show.

steps.title: Judges and counsel
steps.text: Each dot is a judge with at least 25 leave decisions: how often they grant leave, and how often judicial review. Clicking a dot shows only that judge's files. Counsel are listed below in the same way.

steps.title: Filter and explore
steps.text: Every figure on the page now covers only the files filed in the last five years. Further down are timing, deadlines, refusals and the decision makers under review. Rates sit beside their counts, because small groups are not reliable.
steps.say: Filters change every figure at once. I'll press Last 5 years.

steps.title: Your Workbench
steps.text: The Workbench is your own space. The tour signed you in as Demo analyst (no password; a made-up name keeps lists apart). Your case list follows your IMM files, and a flag shows when the Federal Court docket has moved.
steps.leadText: I'll click it in the header.

steps.title: Your saved decision
steps.text: The cessation decision we read is here because the tour saved it from the reader. Saved decisions take folders and notes, and Compare selected sets two side by side.

steps.title: Document tools
steps.text: Two tools work on your own documents: Live analysis reads a factum or memo against the library, and the De-identifier swaps names, ID numbers and dates for placeholders.

steps.title: Your document stays yours
steps.text: Live analysis reads a document you bring, such as a memorandum or a decision, against the library. It is read in memory and dropped: nothing is stored, nothing is sent to an AI model or anywhere outside iLit, and closing the page leaves no copy.
steps.leadText: I'll open it from the Workbench.

steps.title: A Word file, dropped in
steps.text: The file is a fictional Memorandum of Argument from a refugee cessation judicial review, written for this tour. A text PDF works the same way.
steps.say: I'll drag in a Word file, as you would from your desktop.

steps.title: The memo, marked up
steps.text: The counts show the case citations and statute references found, each one marked in the text, and the layer buttons switch them on or off.
steps.say: I'll press Read document.

steps.title: Matched to the library
steps.text: Baker is matched to the decision in the library, with the paragraphs the memo cites (21 to 28). Short forms such as 'Vavilov, above at para 99' and 'Ibid at para 100' are traced back to the case they refer to.

steps.title: Statutes, and what is not held
steps.text: Provisions of IRPA and the Federal Courts Act are found and tied to the statute library. Cases the library does not hold are still marked, so you can see what cannot be checked here.

steps.title: Every authority, and which ones we hold
steps.text: One table of every authority in the document: how it was written, whether it is in the library, and how often it is mentioned. This is the shortlist of cases to read for this argument. It also downloads as a spreadsheet.
steps.say: One table can list every authority in the memo. I'll open it.

steps.title: Pull those cases in one click
steps.text: Every authority in the memo that the library holds is now pinned to your list, ready to open, compare and read.
steps.writes: This step saved the library cases cited in the fictional MOA to the demo Workbench list. Remove them any time from the Workbench.
steps.say: Save library cases to Workbench pins all of them in one go. I'll press it.

steps.title: The result: a reading list from the document
steps.text: The cases cited in the memo that the library holds are now on your Workbench, beside the decision we saved. From here an analyst can open each one, add notes and compare decisions side by side.
steps.lead: Back to the Workbench to see them.

steps.title: How the library keeps up
steps.text: A daily intake job is built. Each run checks the open A2AJ dataset for new Federal Court, Federal Court of Appeal and Supreme Court decisions, adds only the new ones and runs them through the same rule-based processing, and reads the Federal Court registry for new immigration files and docket entries so the statistics stay current. It has been run by hand and is being rolled out to run every night. Refugee Appeal Division decisions are being added now, with newer RPD decisions next.
steps.lead: Last, how the library stays current.
steps.leadText: I'll go back to About, How it works.

steps.title: That is the tour
steps.text: You have seen what iLit is and how it works, search and its filters, the reader, judges, citation intelligence, Federal Court analytics, the Workbench and Live analysis. Take the tour again from the About page whenever you like. Press Done to explore on your own.
